extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of classical Roman literature (Horace), translators and literary scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of Horace's Satires (English translation), extracting prescriptive passages and aphoristic precepts embedded in the poems (e.g., culinary precepts, social/ethical advice, practical arts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Catius's culinary precepts / banqueting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A long series of prescriptive rules about cooking, selecting food, and running a banquet attributed to Catius: e.g., 'Remember to serve up those eggs that are of an oblong make...'; 'Cabbage that grows in dry lands, is sweeter than that about town'; 'drown a tough old hen in Falernian wine...'; 'mushrooms that grow in meadows, are of the best kind'; 'finish his dinners with mulberries black [with ripeness]'; recommendations on which fish, shellfish, and meats are best (Lucrine muscle better than the Baian murex; oysters from the Circaean promontory; cray-fish from Misenum; shoulders of a pregnant hare preferred); and the proper ages/natures of fish and fowl.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed, concrete directives and examples: prefer oblong eggs, prefer dry-land cabbage, tenderize tough hen with Falernian wine, prefer meadow mushrooms, end meals with ripe mulberries, wash the stomach with soft mead, use limpet/coarse cockles and Coan white wine for obstructions, know local provenance of best shellfish and meats, avoid using cheap trays/mats/sawdust carelessly, avoid greasy hands touching cups, preserve the flavor of wine (beware filtration through linen), mix Surrentine wine properly with Falernian lees and collect sediment with a pigeon's egg, know two kinds of sauce (simple: sweet oil; richer sauces with Corycian saffron and Venafran olive oil), and attend to presentation (don't cram roaming fish in a narrow dish). Anti-patterns noted: over-focusing on one detail (e.g., only preventing bad wine while neglecting proper oil), using filthy service, neglecting small inexpensive furnishings that shame you when dirty, and inattentive handling that ruins the guest's experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts of the fortune-hunter (techniques to be named heir)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical tactics, described humorously, for ingratiating oneself with wealthy old men so as to be left legacies: accompany them, present dainties, flatter, act as companion, act as solicitor in suits against wealthier rivals, creep into position as a secondary heir, read wills with a quick glance, collude with managers/freedmen or cunning women, loudly praise any verse or pleasure of the old man, weep and appear faithful, and perform funeral/monument duties handsomely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise behavioural advice and social techniques: present delicacies to the old man first; accept inferior company rather than offend wealthy patrons; be indefatigable in service and visibly useful; act as lawyer/advocate against wealthier claimants, thereby gaining favour; gently manoeuvre into second-heir position so a casualty fills the vacancy; when given a will to read, decline but glimpse contents obliquely; applaud any wretched verse or folly of the old man to inflate his vanity; be judicious in display at funerals and erect monuments without meanness; collude discreetly with household agents. Anti-patterns: being too frank, appearing indifferent, refusing to flatter, or betraying visible joy when the legacy is secured (must disguise emotion). The tone is satirical, so the 'guidance' is presented as worldly, morally dubious tactics rather than commendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for country retirement and its conveniences
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy for a modest country retirement: desire for 'a portion of ground not over large, in which was a garden, and a fountain with a continual stream close to my house, and a little Woodland besides.' Contentment with modest means, avoidance of evil ambition, and enjoyment of simple meals and conversation are promoted over the busy, envious, and obligation-filled life in the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments and examples contrasting rural ease with urban trouble: rural life offers control, leisure for reading and sleep, simple dinner pleasures (beans, herbs larded with bacon), convivial conversation on matters of substance (virtue vs riches), and avoidance of constant civic summons, lawsuits, envy, and petty obligations. Anti-patterns of city life are listed: being hustled as bail, endless appointments, gossip and envy, wasted days in trivial errands, and being 'subjected to envy' for civic proximity. The 'rubric' functions as prescriptive criteria for choosing a life (simplicity, self-sufficiency, measured sociality) and examples of what to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and forms of folly and madness vs. sound life
rubrics_metrics.description: Discursive criteria and illustrative examples used to identify folly or madness: extreme hoarding of wealth and refusing to use it (guarding money that one will not spend), grotesque stinginess (watching a heap of corn but not taking a grain), ostentatious and senseless expenditure to gain applause (spending patrimony to be applauded in public), childish or immoderate behaviour (engaging in games or feminine adornment at age), and excessive passions (love leading to raving or violent acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace contrasts different behaviours to show what true madness is: those who hoard yet starve are mad; those who waste fortune for empty fame are mad; but not all who lack one particular vice are 'sound'—ambition or assuming behaviour is criticized. Numerous illustrative anecdotes (Opimius revived by counting his money, the man who dissolves a pearl in vinegar to swallow it, Ajax killing sheep in a frenzy) supply diagnostic examples. The prose supplies both positive indicators of sanity (using possessions reasonably, moderation) and anti-patterns marking madness (senseless hoarding, childish play in extremes, emotional excesses that lead to crime).
